newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian Occidental mounts rival Wascana bid.
newsitem.headline: Canadian Occidental mounts rival Wascana bid.

text.p: Canadian Occidental Petroleum Ltd. emerged on Tuesday as a white knight for Wascana Energy Inc., making a C$2 billion ($1.5 billion) all-cash bid takeover bid for the company.

The proposal, which would make Calgary-based CanOxy the third largest oil and gas exploration and production company in Canada, eclipsed a hostile C$1.7 billion ($1.2 billion) cash and stock bid by Talisman Energy Inc..
Wascana, which had told investors to expect a rival bidder, said its board of directors was recommending shareholders accept CanOxy's C$20.50 ($14.97) a share offer.

CanOxy is 30 percent-owned by Occidental Petroleum Corp. of Los Angeles. It had been touted by analysts as a top contender for Wascana because of its financial strength, complementary operations in the western Canadian province of Saskatchewan and its need for short-term development prospects to balance high-risk international exploration.

"Not only is this a great operational fit, but this deal puts the excess cash flow being generated by CanOxy to excellent use funding low-risk steady growth," CanOxy Chief Executive David Hentschel told a conference call.
Wascana, based in Regina, Saskatchewan, is a former provincially owned company known mostly for extensive heavy crude oil production in Saskatchewan.
The CanOxy bid represented a 25 percent premium to the closing price of Wascana shares on the Toronto Stock Exchange on Feb. 11, the day before Talisman announced its bid.
It was also 13 percent higher than the share swap value of Talisman's offer of C$18.13 ($13.23) a Wascana share at the close on Monday, the companies said.

Analysts said Talisman would have a difficult time justifying a higher bid, because it would need to top C$21 ($15.33) a share when a two percent break-up fee -- paid to CanOxy if a sweetened bid emerged -- was included.
CanOxy's offer was seen as giving full value to Wascana's assets.
"I'm not (expecting a higher bid) at this point," Matt Janisch, analyst with brokerage Nesbitt Burns, said.

Talisman Chief Executive Jim Buckee said he had yet to decide if his firm would up its offer. But Buckee said the odds of doing so depended on Wascana's allowing Talisman officials to scour confidental financial and operating data, a move Wascana had yet to allow.
"We think that it's not a level playing field -- they're not allowing us to see any data," Buckee said in a telephone interview. "We've signaled that we'd move if we saw value."

CanOxy's Hentschel said his firm would fund the merger from internal cash flow and debt. Cash flow was expected to grow about C$1.20 (88 cents) a share over previous 1997 forecasts to C$6.55 ($4.78), he said.
If the offer went ahead, combined conventional production in 1997 would average about 264,000 barrels of oil equivalent a day worldwide, including 115,000 barrels in Canada.

Under the proposal, Wascana would become a unit of CanOxy and manage both firms' conventional oil and gas assets in western Canada. As in Talisman's offer, Wascana's head office would stay in Regina to fit with Saskatchewan legislation.

Wascana Chief Executive Frank Proto told Reuters he believed Wascana's operations were a better fit for CanOxy than Talisman and that CanOxy had more experience with Wascana's brand of enhanced heavy oil recovery.
Proto said wresting a richer bid was bittersweet because he had proved during the takeover battle that his company's turnaround was well under way.
"I would have rather had other options," he said. "I'm proud of what we've done here, but I'm glad that the value's been recognized."

Investors rushed to grab a piece of the new deal on Tuesday. Wascana shares closed up C$1.10 to C$20.45 in Toronto, topping actives. CanOxy climbed C$1.70 to C$25.15 in second most active trading. Talisman was unchanged at C$43.60, also among actives.
